# Data frames

`RSMutableDataFrame` and `RSDataFrame` wrap R data frames and tibbles as robjc objects.
They store the data internally as a tibble.
These are thin wrappers for working with tabular data. If you need row keys or a hash based on the table's contents, consider defining a class for that purpose.
The standard wrappers provide only the minimum functionality needed to bring data frames and tibbles into robjc's object system.

## Create a data frame object

Pass a data frame or tibble as the `df` argument.
`getDataFrame()` returns the stored tibble.

```{r}
library(robjc)

people <- data.frame(
  id = c(1L, 2L),
  name = c("Ada", "Ben"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
mutable <- RSMutableDataFrame$new(people)
fixed <- RSDataFrame$new(people)

stopifnot(inherits(mutable$getDataFrame(), "tbl_df"))
stopifnot(identical(mutable$getDataFrame(), fixed$getDataFrame()))
stopifnot(mutable$isKindOf(RSDataFrame))
stopifnot(!fixed$isKindOf(RSMutableDataFrame))
```

`RSDataFrame` is the read-only parent class.
Its child, `RSMutableDataFrame`, adds methods for changing the whole table or individual columns.

## Read rows, columns, and dimensions

Use `nrow()`, `ncol()`, `colnames()`, `rownames()`, and `getColumn()` to inspect the table's structure and column values.
The method names correspond to familiar base R functions.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(mutable$nrow(), 2L))
stopifnot(identical(mutable$ncol(), 2L))
stopifnot(identical(mutable$colnames(), c("id", "name")))
stopifnot(identical(mutable$getColumn("name"), c("Ada", "Ben")))
```

## Edit and copy

`setColumn()` changes a column's values, and `setDataFrame()` replaces the whole table.
These methods belong only to `RSMutableDataFrame`; `RSDataFrame` does not provide them.

```{r}
mutable$setColumn("name", c("Ada", "Bea"))
stopifnot(identical(mutable$getColumn("name"), c("Ada", "Bea")))

mutable$setDataFrame(data.frame(id = 3L, name = "Cal", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
stopifnot(identical(mutable$nrow(), 1L))
```

Calling `copy()` on an `RSMutableDataFrame` creates a new, read-only `RSDataFrame`.
Calling `copy()` on an `RSDataFrame` returns that same instance.
For either class, `mutableCopy()` creates a new, editable `RSMutableDataFrame`.
These are shallow copies. R's copy-on-modify behavior means that later changes to a column do not change the original object's table.

```{r}
snapshot <- mutable$copy()
editable <- snapshot$mutableCopy()
editable$setColumn("name", "Dee")

stopifnot(identical(snapshot$getColumn("name"), "Cal"))
stopifnot(identical(editable$getColumn("name"), "Dee"))
```

## Equality, hashing, and archives

`isEqual()` compares the complete stored tibbles with `identical()`.
It distinguishes differences in column values, types, and attributes.
This differs from `==`, which checks whether the wrappers themselves are the same instance.

```{r}
left <- RSMutableDataFrame$new(data.frame(id = 1L, name = "Ada", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
right <- RSDataFrame$new(data.frame(id = 1L, name = "Ada", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
stopifnot(left$isEqual(right))
stopifnot(left != right)
```

> **Note:** DataFrame's `hash()` provides only the minimum support needed to store these objects as Set members or Dictionary keys.
It is not designed to distribute different table values evenly across hashes.

`hash()` uses only the row count, column names, and each column's `typeof()`.
It does not inspect cell values, so different tables with the same structure have the same hash.
Sets and Dictionaries narrow their candidates by hash and then check `isEqual()`, so a collision does not change the equality result.
However, lookup can become slower when many tables with the same structure are stored.

A data frame can contain list columns and values of custom classes as well as ordinary vectors.
Which columns and attributes identify a table, and how far to inspect nested values, depend on the application.
The framework alone cannot choose a **general-purpose hash that is also appropriate for every use case**.
Accordingly, this implementation inspects even nested columns only as far as their `typeof()`.
If you need content-sensitive lookup or row keys, define a class for your use case with a `hash()` consistent with its `isEqual()`.
For a Dictionary key, prefer an `RSDataFrame` whose contents cannot change after insertion.

```{r}
other <- RSDataFrame$new(data.frame(id = 2L, name = "Bea", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
stopifnot(!left$isEqual(other))
stopifnot(identical(left$hash(), other$hash()))
```

The archive stores only the table data.
Column types and values remain available after restoration.
See the [Archiving Guide](guide_10_Archiving.Rmd) for the complete restoration workflow.

```{r}
archive <- RSKeyedArchiver$new()$encode(left)
decoder <- RSKeyedUnarchiver$new(archive)
restored <- decoder$decode()
stopifnot(restored$isEqual(left))
```
